name: Knots & rope
desc: Ten knots drawn step by step, lashing poles together and making cord from plants

s: Working end: the end you tie with. Standing part: the rest of the rope.
Bight: a U-shaped bend in the rope. Loop: a bight where the rope crosses itself.
Hitch: a knot that ties rope to something. Bend: a knot that joins two ropes.
After tying, tidy the knot so nothing is twisted, then pull every part tight.
Leave a tail at least a hand wide.
Practise each knot at home a few times: then your hands remember it when it matters.

guides.w: Stop a rope sliding through a hole
s: Make a loop near the end of the rope.
Pass the working end through the loop.
Pull both ends tight.
It's hard to untie after a load: for a stopper you want to undo later, use a figure-eight.

guides.w: A stopper that's easy to undo
s: Make a loop by laying the working end over the standing part.
Take the end around behind the standing part.
Bring it back to the front and down through the first loop. It now looks like an 8.
Pull tight.
Figure-eight loop: do the same with a bight (doubled rope) to make a strong fixed loop.

guides.w: Tie two ends together: bandage, sling, bundle
s: Right end over left end and under: a first twist.
Then left over right and under: the second twist goes the other way.
Pull both ends: it lies flat and neat.
Remember: right over left, left over right.
Undo it by pushing one end back along its own rope.
d: Don't use it to join two ropes that carry a load: it can slip or tip over (use a sheet bend)

guides.w: Join two ropes, even of different thickness
s: Make a bight (U-shape) in the end of the thicker rope.
Push the thinner rope up through the bight from below.
Take it around behind both legs of the bight.
Tuck it under itself (not through the bight).
Pull tight. Both short ends should end up on the same side.
For slippery rope: go around one more time (double sheet bend).

guides.w: A loop that won't slip or tighten
s: Make a small loop in the standing part, with the working end side on top. This is the rabbit hole; the standing part above is the tree.
The rabbit comes up out of the hole: push the end up through the small loop from underneath.
Around the tree: take the end around behind the standing part.
Back down the hole: push it down through the small loop.
Hold the end and the side of the big loop and pull the standing part to tighten.
Good for a loop around a tree, a person (rescue) or a post. Easy to undo, even after a load.
d: Check it before trusting it with weight: a wrongly tied bowline can slip

guides.w: Quickly tie a rope to a pole or rail
s: Wrap the rope once around the pole.
Cross over the standing part and wrap around again.
Tuck the end under that last wrap, so it comes out between the two wraps.
Pull both ends.
Quick to tie and adjust, but it can slip with a pull from the side: add a half hitch to be safe.

guides.t: Round turn and two half hitches
guides.w: Tie a rope to a ring, tree or post that carries a load
s: Wrap the rope twice around the post or through the ring (a round turn). This takes the load.
Take the end around the standing part and back through: one half hitch.
Do it again in the same direction: two half hitches.
Slide them snug against the round turn.
Easy to undo, even when the rope is tight. Good for tying a boat, a tarp line or a load.

guides.w: An adjustable line for tents and tarps
s: Put the rope around the tent peg or a tree.
Wrap the end twice around the standing part, inside the loop (towards the peg).
Then once more around the standing part, outside the loop.
Pull tight.
Slide the knot along the rope to tighten or loosen the line; it holds where you leave it.

guides.w: For a shelter, a tripod or a stretcher
s: Cross the poles at a right angle.
Tie a clove hitch to the bottom pole, just below the crossing.
Wrap the rope over the top pole, under the bottom pole, over and under again, 3–4 times, keeping it tight.
Then wrap 2–3 times between the poles, around the wraps, pulling hard (frapping): this tightens it all.
Finish with a clove hitch on the other pole.
Use long fibres: the skin of dried nettle stems, long grass, inner bark of lime (linden) or willow, or strips of cloth.
Take a bundle, fold it so one side is longer, and pinch at the fold.
Twist the top strand away from you (clockwise), then lay it over the other strand towards you.
Repeat: twist the new top strand and cross it over. The two strands lock together into cord.
Add new fibres before a strand runs out, overlapping them.
Strong enough for tying shelters, fishing lines and bundles.
